title: Noise-induced classical phases in optimally-unraveled random quantum circuits
authors: Lorenzo Fioroni, Filippo Ferrari, Emanuele Tirrito
abstract: We study the classical simulability of open quantum dynamics using random Clifford circuits doped with non-Clifford phase rotations and subject to local noise. We unravel the dynamics into stochastic quantum trajectories simulated with Clifford-augmented matrix product states, and introduce a simulation cost that quantifies the classical resources required. Optimizing this cost over stochastic unravelings, we identify noise-induced classical phases: extended parameter regions in which the dynamics can be fully disentangled by Clifford operations at arbitrary circuit depth. Their existence depends on both the noise model \emph{and} the unraveling. Using a geometric representation of quantum channels, we analytically determine optimal unravelings for a broad class of noise models, with numerical simulations confirming the predicted phase boundaries. We further relate the optimal cost to the unraveling-independent nonstabilizerness of the channel and show that, together with trajectory-resolved entanglement and nonstabilizerness, it classifies distinct dynamical regimes. Finally, we show that these classical phases disappear in the averaged density-matrix description, where no unraveling freedom remains. Our results show that the emergence of classicality in noisy random circuits depends on the measurement scheme adopted to probe it, and paves the way to further studies on the classical simulability of driven-dissipative dynamics.
summary: This paper studies how noise affects the classical simulability of quantum circuits by analyzing the optimal way to 'unravel' the noisy dynamics into stochastic trajectories. It discovers that noise can create extended 'classical phases' where the system behaves classically, but this classicality is an artifact of the measurement process, not the underlying channel itself. This work provides a resource-theoretic framework for understanding the limits of classical simulation in open quantum systems.
main_problem: The paper investigates the boundary between quantum dynamics that are classically simulable and those that require true quantum computation, particularly in the presence of noise.
main_result: It identifies 'noise-induced classical phases'—parameter regions where the dynamics become fully disentangled by Clifford operations, depending crucially on the measurement scheme (unraveling) used.
method: The authors analyze open quantum dynamics by unraveling them into stochastic quantum trajectories, simulating these using Clifford-augmented matrix product states, and minimizing a derived 'simulation cost.'
model_or_system: The model involves random quantum circuits composed of Clifford gates, non-Clifford phase rotations, and local noise, studied via the evolution of the density matrix.
key_observables: Simulation cost ($ ar{c}$), entanglement, nonstabilizerness, and the optimal unraveling choice.
important_parameters: Noise strength ($p$), non-Clifford density, and the circuit depth ($N_T$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on finding an optimal convex decomposition of the quantum channel and assumes the ability to define an optimal unraveling that minimizes the simulation cost.
figures_summary: Figure 1 sketches the noisy circuit setup and a phase diagram showing three dynamical regions separated by phase boundaries. Other figures illustrate the geometric structure of the channel in the complex plane.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining the problem using noisy random circuits, developing the resource-based simulation cost ($ ar{c}$), analytically determining the optimal unraveling, and contrasting the results obtained from trajectory-based measurements versus the averaged density matrix.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the resource theory of quantum computation, showing how measurement choices (unraveling) can artificially induce classicality, which is highly relevant for understanding decoherence and measurement-induced phase transitions in open quantum systems.
